This is a pilot vignette, to be revised and extended. It compares ASReml and
flexyBayes on one public trial, first as laid out and then reduced in size.
The ASReml results were computed with ASReml 4.2.0.392
under R version 4.5.2 (2025-10-31) on 2026-09-10 by
`data-raw/asreml_reference.R`, and are stored in the package, so this page
builds without an ASReml licence.

# The whole trial

`john.alpha` has 24 genotypes, three replicates, and blocks nested within
replicates. The two calls are written the same way:

| | ASReml | flexyBayes |
|---|---|---|
| model | `asreml(yield ~ rep, random = ~ rep:block + gen, data = john.alpha)` | `flexybayes(yield ~ rep, random = ~ rep:block + gen, data = john.alpha)` |
| heritability | `vpredict(m, h2 ~ V2/(V2 + V3))` | `vpredict(fit, h2 ~ sd_gen^2/(sd_gen^2 + sigma^2))` |


``` r
data(john.alpha, package = "agridat")

fit <- flexybayes(
  fixed   = yield ~ rep,
  random  = ~ rep:block + gen,
  data    = john.alpha,
  backend = "inla",
  verbose = FALSE
)

vpredict(fit, h2 ~ sd_gen^2 / (sd_gen^2 + sigma^2), n_draws = 4000)
#>   functional  estimate    median std.error  conf.low conf.high
#> 1         h2 0.6398204 0.6446432 0.1011168 0.4277483 0.8178433
```

ASReml:


``` r
rnd(asreml_ref$alpha[1, ])
#>                         design  n    h2    se lower upper
#> 1 24 genotypes, 3 reps (whole) 72 0.636 0.108 0.425 0.848
```

Both give a heritability of about 0.64, with similar intervals.

# Smaller trials

The same trial is now reduced, first by keeping fewer genotypes and then by
dropping plots at random. ASReml:


``` r
rnd(asreml_ref$alpha)
#>                           design  n    h2    se  lower upper
#> 1   24 genotypes, 3 reps (whole) 72 0.636 0.108  0.425 0.848
#> 2           12 genotypes, 3 reps 36 0.058 0.302 -0.533 0.649
#> 3            8 genotypes, 3 reps 24 0.177 0.385 -0.578 0.932
#> 4            6 genotypes, 3 reps 18 0.000 0.641 -1.256 1.256
#> 5 25% of plots dropped at random 54 0.491 0.179  0.141 0.841
#> 6 50% of plots dropped at random 36 0.408 0.305 -0.190 1.006
#> 7 65% of plots dropped at random 25 0.476 0.278 -0.069 1.020
```

With 12 genotypes the lower limit is -0.53.
With 6 genotypes the interval runs from -1.26
to 1.26. A heritability lies between 0 and
1, so these limits are outside its range. They come from the delta method,
whose normal approximation fails when a variance component is near zero.

flexyBayes on the same designs:


``` r
degrade <- function(n_gen = NULL, drop_frac = NULL) {
  d <- john.alpha
  if (!is.null(n_gen)) {
    d <- droplevels(subset(d, gen %in% levels(d$gen)[seq_len(n_gen)]))
  }
  if (!is.null(drop_frac)) {
    set.seed(2026)
    d <- droplevels(d[-sample(nrow(d), round(drop_frac * nrow(d))), ])
  }
  d
}

designs <- list(
  "24 genotypes, 3 reps (whole)"    = degrade(),
  "12 genotypes, 3 reps"            = degrade(n_gen = 12),
  "6 genotypes, 3 reps"             = degrade(n_gen = 6),
  "50% of plots dropped at random"  = degrade(drop_frac = 0.50),
  "65% of plots dropped at random"  = degrade(drop_frac = 0.65)
)

out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(designs), function(nm) {
  f <- flexybayes(yield ~ rep, random = ~ rep:block + gen,
                  data = designs[[nm]], backend = "inla", verbose = FALSE)
  v <- vpredict(f, h2 ~ sd_gen^2 / (sd_gen^2 + sigma^2), n_draws = 4000)
  data.frame(design = nm, n = nrow(designs[[nm]]),
             h2 = v$estimate, lower = v$conf.low, upper = v$conf.high)
}))
rnd(out)
#>                           design  n    h2 lower upper
#> 1   24 genotypes, 3 reps (whole) 72 0.640 0.428 0.817
#> 2           12 genotypes, 3 reps 36 0.678 0.381 0.894
#> 3            6 genotypes, 3 reps 18 0.756 0.374 0.965
#> 4 50% of plots dropped at random 36 0.383 0.049 0.806
#> 5 65% of plots dropped at random 25 0.276 0.012 0.764
```

Every interval lies between 0 and 1, because every posterior draw does. The
intervals for the reduced designs are wider than for the whole trial.

With 6 genotypes the data say little about the genetic variance. ASReml
estimates it as zero, while the posterior stays away from zero because of
the prior. If the true genetic variance were near zero, the prior would hold
the estimate too high. The posterior interval is not guaranteed to be right,
but it contains only possible values.

# Summary

On the whole trial the two methods agree. On smaller trials, and for
quantities near a boundary such as a small variance, the posterior interval
stays within the parameter's range and the delta-method interval may not.
